name: The Theory of Ideas (Forms)
plain_explanation: Behind every group of things that share a common name (all cats, all beds, all beautiful things), there is, Plato argues, a single, eternal, perfect 'Idea' or 'Form' -- the real cat, the real bed -- of which the many particular examples are only imperfect copies.
precise_definition: Plato's doctrine, partly logical and partly metaphysical, that general words signify not particular things but a single, timeless, non-spatial universal nature ('cattyness,' the Idea of Beauty, the Idea of Bed) in which particulars 'participate' imperfectly; the metaphysical elaboration adds that each Idea is a single perfect object created by God.
why_it_mattered: Russell treats it as 'the first theory to emphasise the problem of universals,' the question of what, if anything, general words refer to -- a problem that 'has persisted to the present day.'
historical_origin: The logical part responds to the plain fact that language needs general words; the metaphysical part is Plato's own addition, not traceable to Parmenides or the Pythagoreans.
examples: The 'ideal cat' created by God, of which all particular cats are imperfect copies.
The one real bed made by God, as opposed to the many beds made by carpenters, illustrated by the last book of the Republic's discussion of painters and mirrors.
objections: Russell: Plato does not understand philosophical syntax -- he treats 'beauty is beautiful' as sensible, when in fact a universal like 'human' cannot sensibly be predicated of itself; Plato's Ideas end up being just superior particulars, not genuine universals.

The problem of the 'third man': if a particular resembles its Idea, a further Idea is needed to explain that resemblance, and so on ad infinitum (raised by Parmenides against Socrates in the dialogue Parmenides).
competing_positions: The minimal, purely logical claim -- that general and relational words are meaningful and cannot be reduced to proper names -- which Russell says he is willing to accept, while rejecting the full metaphysical doctrine.
influence_on_later_thinkers: Influenced 'most of the great philosophers, down to and including Hegel'; later medieval disputes over universals (realism vs. nominalism) descend from it.
